topics.reason: The particle contributes vocative attention rather than root meaning.

topics.headline: three-part vocative chain begins
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the decision frame grounded in a formal title before the alternatives appear.
topics.reason: The sequence opens the particle plus possessor noun plus genitive title chain.

topics.headline: open-vowel address cadence
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears a slowed entrance before the binary options.
topics.reason: The phonetic row notes the long open vowels at the start of the address.

words.gloss_range: vocative form of the possessor noun, making the following dual title the addressee's characterization
words.prose: {{ar:ذَا}} ({{tr:dhā}}) cannot stand alone; it makes the following dual title the way the addressee is identified. In the vocative form of the five nouns, possession becomes characterization rather than mere ownership. That title then controls the second-person verbs of punishment and adopting goodness, and the same titled address links the section's introduction, divine address, and later appeal at 18:83, 18:86, and 18:94.
words.root_gloss_range: possession, having, and being characterized by an attached attribute; local vocative form selects titled characterization

topics.headline: vocative five-noun form with genitive complement
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices a marked address form built to carry the title.
topics.reason: The form is vocative and depends on the following genitive complement.

topics.headline: possession as identity-marker
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Dhū al-Qarnayn addressed by an attribute that defines his role at the decision moment.
topics.reason: The possessor sense is narrowed from ownership to titular characterization.

topics.headline: title refrain across narrative nodes
topics.reader_payoff: The reader connects this address to the title at 18:83 and 18:94.
topics.reason: The title appears at introduction, divine address, and later public appeal.

words.gloss_range: definite dual genitive title complement, carrying paired horns/peaks/epochs and twofold identity pressure
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْقَرْنَيْنِ}} ({{tr:al-qarnayni}}) completes the title in a definite dual form. The grammar marks the qarnayn as the attribute by which the addressee is known, while the dual form makes twoness explicit before the two-option frame arrives. Horn, peak, epoch, and pairing pressures remain title-density, not a replacement for the proper epithet; the title also recurs as a narrative marker at 18:83, 18:86, and 18:94, with the companion sense in 43:36 kept only as pairing pressure.
words.root_gloss_range: horn, peak, generation or epoch, pairing, joining, and companionship; local title selects the definite dual epithet

topics.headline: definite dual genitive completes the title
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the title is grammatically complete and specifically dual.
topics.reason: The noun is definite, dual, and genitive after the possessor noun.

topics.headline: dense qarn range inside the title
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the epithet as emblematic, spatial, temporal, and paired without reducing it to one gloss.
topics.reason: The local title can carry horn, peak, epoch, and pairing pressure while remaining a proper epithet.

topics.headline: dual title prepares binary choice
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees a twofold title meet a twofold moral option while remaining a title refrain across 18:83, 18:86, and 18:94.
topics.reason: The dual morphology is followed by the paired immā options.

words.gloss_range: first disjunctive particle opening the either-branch and making punishment one option inside a binary
words.prose: {{ar:إِمَّآ}} ({{tr:immā}}) opens the decision frame by making punishment one branch of an either-or structure. The first particle is visibly incomplete until its matching partner arrives, so the speech is organized as a controlled binary rather than an open command. Its conditional coloring keeps the action as a possible course for the addressed agent, and the geminated mīm gives both openings of the binary a pressed sound.

topics.headline: first particle opens disjunctive scope
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that punishment is one branch, not the whole instruction.
topics.reason: The particle scopes over the following complementizer and verb.

topics.headline: either-force with conditional coloring
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the option as selectable rather than asserted as a fact.
topics.reason: The particle functions as either while retaining possible conditional force.

topics.headline: paired particle anticipates the second branch
topics.reader_payoff: The reader waits for the matching second option as soon as the first particle appears.
topics.reason: The repeated particle creates the immā...wa-immā frame.

topics.headline: geminated mīm locks the choice
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears formal pressure binding the two options.
topics.reason: The phonetic row ties the shaddah to the paired decision frame.

words.gloss_range: subjunctive complementizer turning punishing into the content-unit of the first option
words.prose: {{ar:أَنْ}} ({{tr:an}}) makes the punishment verb into the content of the first option. It governs the subjunctive and turns the action into a selectable course, not a stand-alone assertion. Because the same particle returns in the second branch, the two alternatives receive matching syntactic scaffolding.

topics.headline: complementizer governs the first subjunctive verb
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the first option as a governed clause, not an independent command.
topics.reason: The particle governs the following subjunctive verb.

topics.headline: action nominalized as an option-unit
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees punishing packaged as one selectable course.
topics.reason: The maṣdariyya function turns the following action into option content.

topics.headline: first template for the repeated complementizer
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees both branches prepared as syntactically equal.
topics.reason: The first complementizer establishes the pattern repeated before the adoption verb.

words.gloss_range: subjunctive second-person Form II punitive action, with the people implied as patient inside the first option
words.prose: {{ar:تُعَذِّبَ}} ({{tr:tuʿadhdhiba}}) gives the first branch its action: the addressee may punish. The subjunctive keeps the act inside the option, the second-person form assigns agency to Dhū al-Qarnayn, and the missing object is recoverable as the discovered people. Form II makes the punishment deliberate and intensive, while the root's fresh-water derivative creates a lexical tension beside the muddy spring without displacing the punitive sense. The same root is taken up in 18:87 when the response specifies how this branch will be used.
words.root_gloss_range: punishment, torment, discipline, and a sweet/fresh-water derivative; local Form II selects deliberate punitive infliction

topics.headline: subjunctive second-person action with implied object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices delegated agency and a compressed patient: you may punish them.
topics.reason: The verb is governed by the complementizer, second masculine singular, and has an implied object referring to the people.

topics.headline: punitive action selected over generic harm
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees one pole of governance as deliberate punishment, not random injury, with a fresh-water lexical tension sounding beside the spring scene.
topics.reason: The local binary and Form II morphology select punish or discipline.

topics.headline: punishment branch answered in the next ayah
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees this option immediately carried forward into 18:87.
topics.reason: The same root appears in Dhū al-Qarnayn's response at 18:87.

topics.headline: gemination makes intensity audible
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the intensive morphology in the doubled middle radical.
topics.reason: The phonetic and form rows connect shaddah with Form II punitive force.

words.gloss_range: connector inside the disjunctive pair, pivoting from punishment to the constructive alternative
words.prose: {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) works inside the paired either-or construction, so it is not simple addition. It joins the two branches by separating them: punishment on one side, adopted goodness on the other. The connector is the hinge where the decision turns from punitive action toward constructive action.

topics.headline: connector inside wa-immā disjunction
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices an or-function carried by an additive-looking particle.
topics.reason: Inside the immā...wa-immā construction, the conjunction coordinates alternatives.

topics.headline: binding and dividing at once
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the two options held in one frame while kept distinct.
topics.reason: The particle form joins, but the construction makes the value disjunctive.

topics.headline: pivot from punishment to goodness
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the moral turn occur at the connector itself.
topics.reason: The conjunction stands between the punishment branch and the adoption-of-goodness branch.

topics.headline: balanced binary cadence
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the midpoint of a two-part frame.
topics.reason: The phonetic row identifies the immā...wa-immā cadence.

words.gloss_range: second disjunctive particle closing the paired frame and introducing the constructive branch
words.prose: The second {{ar:إِمَّآ}} ({{tr:immā}}) completes the binary opened by the first. It introduces adopting goodness as the true alternative to punishment, not as an afterthought or supplement. Repetition of the same geminated form makes the branches symmetrical on the surface even though their moral directions differ.

topics.headline: second particle closes the disjunctive scope
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices a complete two-option decision space.
topics.reason: The second particle introduces the matched alternative branch.

topics.headline: constructive option as alternative, not supplement
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees goodness as the other branch rather than an addition after punishment.
topics.reason: Its placement before the adoption verb frames that action as the alternative to punishment.

topics.headline: mirrored particle, different content
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees surface symmetry carry semantic contrast.
topics.reason: The repeated particle mirrors the first while the branch content changes.

topics.headline: paired gemination brackets the alternatives
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the two options locked into one controlled frame.
topics.reason: The doubled mīm recurs in both particles.

words.gloss_range: second complementizer giving the adoption branch the same subjunctive dependency as the punishment branch
words.prose: The second {{ar:أَنْ}} ({{tr:an}}) gives the goodness branch the same grammatical form as the punishment branch. It governs the adoption verb and turns adopting goodness into one selectable action-unit. The syntax is symmetrical even though the moral content is not.

topics.headline: second complementizer governs adoption
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices equal syntactic footing for the constructive branch.
topics.reason: The particle governs the following subjunctive adoption verb.

topics.headline: adopting packaged as an option-unit
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the whole adoption phrase as a selectable course.
topics.reason: The maṣdariyya function packages the action as option content.

topics.headline: complementizer symmetry across branches
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees moral contrast carried in parallel clause form.
topics.reason: The second complementizer repeats the first before a different verb.

words.gloss_range: subjunctive Form VIII adopting or instituting goodness among the people, not seizing them as object
words.prose: {{ar:تَتَّخِذَ}} ({{tr:tattakhidha}}) makes the second option active: he may adopt or institute goodness among the people. The people are not the thing taken; the following prepositional phrase makes them the domain, while goodness is the object. Form VIII keeps the take-root deliberate and policy-like, contrasting constructive adoption with the punishment branch. It also joins a Kahf taking or adopting motif at 18:4, 18:15, 18:50, 18:77, 18:79, and 18:102; here the taking is authorized toward goodness, especially against the disobedience frame around divine speech at 18:50.
words.root_gloss_range: taking, seizing, adopting, taking for oneself, and instituting; local Form VIII with goodness object selects deliberate adoption

topics.headline: verb takes domain phrase plus abstract object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that goodness is the object and the people are the domain.
topics.reason: Local valency combines the adoption verb with a prepositional domain and an accusative goodness object.

topics.headline: adoption selected over seizure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the take-root rerouted from capture into constructive institution.
topics.reason: Form VIII and the goodness object select deliberate adoption rather than physical seizure.

topics.headline: authorized taking within the Kahf motif
topics.reader_payoff: The reader connects this taking to a surah-local pattern while seeing it authorized toward goodness here.
topics.reason: The rows cite forms of the root at 18:4, 18:15, 18:50, 18:77, 18:79, and 18:102.

words.gloss_range: preposition plus plural suffix marking the people as the domain in which or concerning which goodness is adopted
words.prose: {{ar:فِيهِمْ}} ({{tr:fīhim}}) makes the discovered people the domain of the goodness branch without making them the object taken. The plural suffix retrieves the earlier collective people, while the preposition places the action among or concerning them. Its local echo of the earlier in-phrase shifts containment from the cosmic spring to a social field.

topics.headline: domain complement, not direct object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the people are where the adopted goodness operates, not what is adopted.
topics.reason: The phrase attaches to the adoption verb while the goodness noun remains the object.

topics.headline: among and concerning both fit the action
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the goodness as internal to the community and directed with respect to them.
topics.reason: The preposition can mark among or concerning, and both are locally licensed.

topics.headline: second fī shifts from cosmic to social containment
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the ayah reuse containment language for ethical action among people.
topics.reason: The local reprise links the spring frame at word 8 with the people-domain at word 26.

words.gloss_range: indefinite verbal noun object of adoption, naming open-ended goodness, beauty, and excellence as the constructive option
words.prose: {{ar:حُسْنًۭا}} ({{tr:ḥusnan}}) is the thing adopted in the second branch. As an indefinite verbal noun, it names goodness or excellence without reducing it to one policy, and the root keeps beauty and moral goodness together. It stands opposite the intensive punishment verb, so the contrast is not only punitive versus lenient but inflicted punishment versus adopted excellence; 18:88 then takes up the goodness field again.
words.root_gloss_range: goodness, beauty, excellence, doing well, and beneficence; local verbal noun selects an adoptable quality rather than a single counted deed

topics.headline: maṣdar object of adoption
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that goodness itself is the adopted object.
topics.reason: The noun is accusative as the object of the adoption verb.

topics.headline: beauty and moral goodness fused
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the constructive option as excellent and beautifying, not merely procedurally nice.
topics.reason: The root field joins goodness, beauty, and excellence in the local object.

topics.headline: goodness branch balances punishment and is taken up forward
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the positive branch positioned against punishment and continued in 18:88.
topics.reason: The binary contrasts the Form II punishment verb with the goodness verbal noun, and the root recurs in 18:88.

topics.headline: tanwīn cadence links people and goodness
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the discovered people tied to the positive object through matching accusative endings.
topics.reason: The phonetic row pairs qawman and ḥusnan by final tanwīn.
